analysis.one_liner: Makes asbestos and silica lawsuits much harder to win and caps victims' damages.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made asbestos lawsuits much harder to win and capped victims' damages at $250,000, gathered 62 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for asbestos and silica lawsuits nationwide. People exposed to asbestos but not yet sick could not sue at all, and even sick workers would have had to meet strict new medical criteria to get to court. It would have capped payments for pain and suffering at $250,000 (double for mesothelioma), banned punitive damages entirely, moved all cases into federal court, limited which courts could hear them, and applied all of this retroactively to cases already filed that had not reached final judgment.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that made, sold, installed, or used asbestos products, along with their insurers and owners of buildings containing asbestos. They would face far fewer lawsuits, lower maximum payouts, no punitive damages, and a rule that each defendant pays only its exact share of fault — including shares assigned to companies already in bankruptcy that victims could never collect from. The bill's stated purpose was to keep these companies solvent so they could pay the sickest claimants and protect their employees' jobs and pensions.

how_it_helps.text: Shields companies facing asbestos liability by requiring proof of actual physical impairment before anyone can sue, capping noneconomic damages at $250,000 ($500,000 for mesothelioma), and banning punitive damages outright.

Moves every asbestos and silica case into federal court and limits venue to the plaintiff's home district or where the exposure occurred, taking cases away from state courts that defendants considered plaintiff-friendly.

Shields product sellers, renters, lessors, and premises owners from most liability, leaving them responsible only in narrow circumstances such as negligence, an independent warranty, or intentional wrongdoing.

Preserves defendants' finances by the bill's own stated logic: its findings cite more than 70 asbestos-driven bankruptcies and argue that paying exposed-but-unsick claimants threatens companies' ability to compensate cancer victims and endangers workers' jobs, benefits, and savings.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and their families sickened by asbestos or silica exposure. People exposed but not yet impaired could no longer sue. Workers with nonmalignant disease would have to meet rigid medical thresholds — specific breathing-test results and chest X-rays graded by a certified reader — to get into court. Smokers with lung cancer would have needed both evidence of asbestosis and a certified industrial-hygienist exposure reconstruction. Recoveries for pain and suffering would be capped, punitive damages eliminated, awards reduced by any other compensation received, and all of it applied to cases already pending.

drawbacks.text: The medical gatekeeping is so strict that many genuinely sick workers would never reach a jury: a nonmalignant claim requires at minimum Class 2 respiratory impairment, a qualifying chest X-ray read by a certified B-reader, and specific lung-volume test results, all from a physician with tightly limited litigation work.

The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies to the total award no matter how many defendants are sued, and punitive damages — the main tool for punishing companies that concealed asbestos hazards — are banned entirely.

The bill applies retroactively to every pending case without a final judgment, giving plaintiffs already in litigation as little as 60 days to produce reports meeting the new evidentiary standards or see their claims dismissed.

Supporters' strongest argument is real: asbestos litigation had driven more than 70 companies into bankruptcy, and paying millions of exposed-but-unsick claimants could leave future cancer victims uncompensated. But the bill goes well beyond triaging the sickest claimants — it also strips damages from people who clearly are sick and eliminates accountability for misconduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — reserving limited defendant assets for the most seriously ill — addresses a genuine problem, since mass asbestos litigation had bankrupted dozens of companies. But the design weights that goal heavily toward defendants: rigid diagnostic screens that exclude many sick workers, a total punitive-damages ban, a flat cap on suffering regardless of how many companies caused the harm, and retroactive application to cases already in court. The savings flow mainly to the companies and insurers paying claims, not to the victims being told to wait.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Cannon introduced the bill on April 28, 2005 with 41 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee.
The bill drew 62 cosponsors in total, all of them Republicans.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed: the action history shows nothing after the referral to the Judiciary Committee, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People sickened by asbestos and their families came out ahead: they kept their existing right to sue in state court with uncapped damages, no new diagnostic hurdles, and no retroactive deadlines. Defendants and insurers gained nothing, but they also lost nothing — they remain liable under pre-existing law.

for.name: Chris Cannon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 41 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 62 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

against.name: F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the committee took no action after the April 2005 referral.

against.name: Labor unions and asbestos victims' advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed legislation during the 2005 asbestos debate that would restrict asbestos victims' access to the courts and cap their compensation.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; all 62 cosponsors were Republicans, while the parallel asbestos fight of that era split both parties internally.

industries.industry: Asbestos manufacturers, premises owners, and product sellers (defendants)
industries.note: The bill would hand these companies far fewer lawsuits, proof requirements that exclude many sick claimants, capped damages, a punitive-damages ban, and liability only for their exact share of fault — including fault assigned to bankrupt companies victims cannot collect from. Its savings come directly out of recoveries for sick workers.
Insurers stand behind asbestos defendants' liabilities; caps on noneconomic damages, elimination of punitive damages, and higher proof thresholds would sharply cut their payouts.

The bill targets screening clinics and law firms that recruit exposed-but-unsick clients, bans reliance on mass screenings lacking a doctor-patient relationship, and limits fees by shrinking the pool of viable claims. Their interest in this bill ran alongside their clients' access to compensation.
